query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermal annealing of as-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys induces a phase transformation from a metastable mix of solid solution and intermetallic compounds into a more equilibrium microstructure with segregated, Mg‐poor intermetallic phases, thereby enhancing the alloy’s ability to form protective surface films that improve corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a heterogeneous microstructure exhibiting metastable solid solution and intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled thermal annealing protocol (via a programmed temperature ramp under fixed oxygen partial pressure) to promote phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Alloy samples with densities below 6 g/cm³ are annealed under fixed oxygen partial pressures and subjected to a pre-determined temperature ramp; subsequent oxidation and corrosion tests are conducted under identical environmental conditions for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation and segregation of metastable intermetallic phases leading to a refined, Mg-poor intermetallic network and a more stable solid solution.
generation.mechanism: The thermal energy provided during annealing accelerates atomic diffusion, resulting in the coarsening and re-distribution of intermetallic phases. This process reduces Mg concentration at grain boundaries, facilitating the formation of a coherent and protective oxide film during high-temperature exposure and enhancing passivation behavior during corrosion tests.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, annealed specimens will show reduced corrosion current density, increased corrosion potential, and slower mass gain in high-temperature oxidation tests due to the formation of a more stable and protective microstructure.
generation.baseline: The as-cast state featuring a metastable microstructure with mixed solid solution and intermetallic compounds.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ processed under controlled oxygen partial pressures; deviations in cooling rates or environmental oxygen levels may alter the transformation pathway and protective film formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of the phase evolution on corrosion and oxidation behaviors is not fully determined, and additional in-situ microstructural characterization is needed to verify the specific intermetallic changes and their distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy specimens (density <6 g/cm³): one in the as-cast state and one subjected to the specified thermal annealing treatment. Expose both groups to identical high-temperature oxidation and electrochemical corrosion test conditions.
measurements: In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) during annealing to monitor phase evolution and verify the formation of Mg-poor intermetallic networks.
Electrochemical tests to measure corrosion potential and corrosion current density.
High-temperature oxidation tests to determine mass gain rates and oxide scale integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion potential (i.e., higher values) and a reduction in corrosion current density, as well as a lower oxidation rate (mass gain) compared to the as-cast specimens, or if in-situ XRD fails to detect the anticipated phase transformation, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCrx coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr1) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 []. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [,,,,]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [,,]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [,,,]. This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. The alloys JZ1 and JZ2 had lower Ge and Sn concentrations and the same but lower Ti concentrations than the alloys studied by Vellios and Tsakiropoulos (see []) and Li and Tsakiropoulos [] and references within and did not suffer from complete disintegration to powders, instead their scales spalled off and scale fragments disintegrated into powder. This suggests (i) that the simultaneous presence of Ge and Sn in the alloys “controlled and improved” the effect of Ge and (ii) that the synergy of these two elements with Hf, Ta, Ti, and W was also beneficial regarding control of pest oxidation. The oxidation resistance of the alloy JZ2 at 800 °C was slightly improved, most likely because of its lower vol.% of the Nbss and higher Sn+Ge content, compared with the alloy JZ1. The results of this work and the literature suggest that additional research should aim to find out whether the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys with Ta and W additions in the pest regime could be improved with simultaneous addition of Sn and Ge with Al and Cr.

The (Nb,Ti,Cr)5(Si,Ge)3 exhibits the highest hardness. The hardness of the silicide in the alloys JZ3 and JZ3+, respectively was 1712 ± 40 and 1826 ± 54 HV.

In this work, alloy Nb–30Ti–10Si–5Cr–5Sn–3Fe–2Al–2Hf (NV2) was studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions: its isothermal oxidation at three pest oxidation temperatures and its room temperature hardness and specific strength were evaluated and compared with other Sn-containing RM(Nb)ICs—in particular, alloy NV5—and with RCCAs and RHEAs. The issues that motivated this research were resolved. The synergy of Fe with Al, Cr, Hf and Sn (a) stabilised Nbss; A15–Nb3X (X = Al, Si and Sn) and Nb3Si, metastable Nb3Si-m’ and Nb5Si3 silicides; (b) supported the formation of Nbss + Nb5Si3 eutectic in the cast microstructure; (c) suppressed pest oxidation in the temperature range 700–900 °C and (d) stabilised a Cr-rich π phase instead of a C14–Nb(Cr,Fe)2 Laves phase. Furthermore, it was shown that complex concentrated (CC) or high entropy (HE) phases coexisted with “conventional” phases in all conditions and after oxidation at 800 °C.
